README: What sclaude knows about a project. Copy this into the repository as
.sclaude/config.json and commit it: it describes the project, so it belongs to
the project rather than to the orchestrator. `sclaude new` offers to write
one by reading package.json, the directory layout and whatever the project
keeps about its environments — this file is for the parts it could not
work out, and for reading before you agree to what it proposes.
Every section is optional and nothing is guessed at run time. What is
absent is simply not done: no `regression` means no gate on step 2, no
`manuals` means step 1 gets no table of contents, no `prod` means
production is never offered. A default would be one product's answer
applied to another's repository, which is the failure this file removes.
commands  — the command behind each regression part. The names on the
left are sclaude's: they appear beside durations in the
summary and in 'failed on X'. `e2e` is the only one sclaude
touches — against a deployed stage it is prefixed with
E2E_BASE_URL=<host> exported, so one command serves both. Every
part also gets SCLAUDE_DEV=<name> exported when sclaude knows
who is running it (developer.sh): a suite that creates test
data on a shared database can mark it with the name and sweep
only its own, instead of deleting a colleague's mid-run.
regression — which parts each stage runs, in order. `local` closes step 2
against this machine's dev server; `preview` and `prod` run
against a deployment and usually hold only what a browser can
see. A part named here with no entry in `commands` stops the
run rather than being skipped: a suite that quietly drops a
check reports green on work it never did.
`manual` is what the end of the review runs instead of
`local` when nothing but the `manuals` changed since the last
green local run — checks that read the code, since a manual is
code too. The dev server and database are not brought up for
it, so leave out anything that needs them. Absent or empty,
the full `local` list runs.
manuals   — the pages describing the product as a person sees it. Step 1
gets their contents before it guesses at the scope; step 3
updates them in the same pull request as the feature.
database  — everything about migrations; leave it out if there are none.
A rollback reads production's database URL from its .env file
(environments) and never prints it. historyTable is where the migration
tool records what it has applied; a reverted migration's row
is deleted with it, or the next promote refuses. Name it only
if you know it: a guessed table that a rollback deletes from
is worse than a row left behind.
`local` gives a feature on the local environment a Supabase
stack of its own: `environment` names that environment,
`exclude` the containers a feature does not need, `setup` the
command that fills a new stack, and `env` maps each of your
variables to the `supabase status -o env` key that fills it.
`cli` overrides how the CLI is run (npx --yes supabase).
board     — the GitHub project board. `columns` names which column a
started feature leaves (backlog) and enters (progress),
where it goes once the preview is green (qa) and where QA
passes it (done). `dates` names the issue date fields filled
at the start and the end. `issue` is the label and type a new
issue gets. Every key optional: a column not named is a move
not made, and nothing here is assumed about your board.
doctor    — what the project asks of a developer's machine beyond what
sclaude checks: each `check` runs in the project's root, and
`sclaude doctor` shows ✓ when it exits 0, or ! with its last
line and the `fix` to run. Warnings only: a developer may
reasonably do without a project's extras.
environments — the project's databases, each the .env file that holds
it, relative to the repository's root. A tree is on the one
its .env.local points at; sclaude switches it by pointing
.env.local elsewhere and, on Supabase, linking the CLI to the
project that file's URL names. Credentials stay in the files;
what sclaude needs it reads from there, and asks at the
terminal when no file says. `protected` marks real data: no
feature is pointed there and no session may switch a tree to
production; its `siteUrl` is where production answers.
`deployed` marks one with no fixed address, such as previews,
which a local dev server does not run against. `envKeys`
renames the keys read from the files: `supabaseUrl`
(NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL), `database`
(POSTGRES_URL_NON_POOLING) and `secretKey`
(SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY, for devLogin).
devLogin  — sign a feature's browser in with one click. `path` is the
product's route for email links, the one that takes
`token_hash`, `type` and `next` and verifies them. With it the
list at localhost:3000 and the bot's Mini App open a feature
signed in: sclaude-proxy asks the feature's Supabase for a
magic-link token and sends the browser there. Who it signs in
as is each developer's own, never committed: the first line of
~/.claude/sclaude/dev-login, else their git user.email. Never
on a protected environment.
maintainers — the git addresses of the people who keep this project's
shared sclaude rules, in .sclaude/team/. Everybody else's
sessions put theirs in .sclaude/people/<name>/, and a hook
keeps them out of team/; a maintainer lifts a rule from there.
Absent or empty, everybody is a maintainer: what a project with
one developer wants.
review    — where the pull request's review runs: "github" (the
review workflow in Actions; the default, and what any word
sclaude does not know means), "local" (sclaude runs the same
/code-review on this machine at step 4, under the Claude
account logged in here, and gives the findings to the session:
tokens, but no Actions minutes) or "off".
The last two open the pull request labelled no-review, the
workflow's own switch, so it skips itself at no cost.

manuals.what: user-facing — what a person can do
